sources.title: Raden Saleh (Q1375979), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-04): English label 'Raden Saleh', description 'painter from Indonesia (1811-1880)', died 1880-04-23, birth year recorded as 1811 with alternatives 1814 and 1807, Korean label present. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam, object SK-A-4703 'Portrait of Raden Syarif Bustaman Saleh' (attributed to Friedrich Carl Albert Schreuel, c. 1840), museum label text read in the linked-art record: a scion of a Javanese regent family who came to the Netherlands in 1829 to train as a painter; shown here as a European dandy before a Western seascape, but he soon specialised in oriental scenes and dressed as a Javanese prince; back on Java (1851) he built a small neo-Gothic palace where he received the European elite; the label says he constantly shifted between his Javanese and European identity. A short museum text; the image record itself carries a Public Domain Mark and CC0.

Niken Prathivi, 'An encounter with Raden Saleh', The Jakarta Post, 13 January 2013, read in full: an interview with the curator and biographer Werner Kraus, who calls Saleh an exceptional personality and the first educated Indonesian to reach Europe and the first to study art there, speaking at least four European languages and at home in both European and Javanese culture; says he was technically as good as or better than his European contemporaries, helped create German Orientalism in Dresden, and after returning to Java founded his own school of landscape painting while cut off from international developments; names the Arrest of Prince Diponegoro as Kraus's favourite work. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE (together with the Rijksmuseum label). Kraus is the exhibition curator and author of the main monograph, so admiring and promotional.

Dina Indrasafitri, "Raden Saleh's masterpieces on display at National Gallery", The Jakarta Post, 31 May 2012, read in full: coverage of the 2012 Jakarta exhibition 'Raden Saleh and the Beginning of Modern Indonesian Painting' (over 40 works, curated by Werner Kraus), calling him 'father of Indonesian modernity', saying he went to Europe at about 18 and spent over 20 years there, and describing him as also an architect, landscape gardener and collector of ethnographic and archaeological documents, who tried to introduce modernity to cultural and scientific fields, with a flamboyant, self-designed dress style; notes that the show opened amid allegations of widespread forgery of works by Indonesian masters. Exhibition-promotion coverage.

Dina Indrasafitri, "Getting to know the 'Maestro'", The Jakarta Post, 12 June 2012, read in full: a profile based on the curator Werner Kraus; born in Semarang in 1811, left for Europe in 1829, first exhibited at the National Exhibition in Amsterdam in 1834, more than 20 years in Europe, felt unwelcome in the Netherlands but accepted in high-standing German families, settled in Germany and learned German, and is quoted as saying he came to Europe as a Javanese but returned to Java as a real German; on return he was warmly received but troubled by colonial racial prejudice; Kraus rejected offered works he did not consider genuine. Curator-sourced and sympathetic.

Sarah Wiertz, 'The Father of Indonesian Painting', Qantara.de (Deutsche Welle's dialogue portal, undated), read in full: born on Java; the Belgian painter Antoine Payen recognised his talent and helped him win a scholarship to study in the Netherlands in 1830; trained and sent on study trips across Europe by the Dutch government; chose to stay in Dresden, where commissions let him work independently; fluent in five languages; recalled Saxony as the best time of his life; called back to Java in 1851, where he painted Javanese scenes, worked as a lay archaeologist and joined an expedition in Central Java; painted lions and tigers probably observed at a zoo or circus because lions do not live on Java; regarded as a founder of German Orientalism and the father of Indonesian painting. A popular article with no listed sources; some details conflict with other sources (study start 1829/1830, five versus four languages).

Sotheby's Hong Kong, catalogue note 'Raden Saleh's Life and Work' for the 2017 Modern and Contemporary Art Evening Sale (lot 1026, 'Fighting Animals', c. 1850), read in full: arrival in the Netherlands in 1829 and a royal stipend; 22 years in Europe before returning to Java in 1852; the title 'King's Painter' from William II in 1850; his search for subject matter beyond portraiture and his study of the animals of the trainer Henri Martin's menagerie; quotes a letter from his friend M. E. Verstege (cited to Kraus and Vogelsang, 2012, p. 40) saying Saleh lost his friendship for a time by neglecting his obligations and painting Martin's portrait for free to get to paint his lions. An auction-house sales essay, so promotional; the note's date for the Martin show ('1937') is an evident misprint and is not used.

Elly Kent, 'Stealing Raden Saleh: War and Art in Indonesia', Perspectives Magazine, National Gallery Singapore (26 March 2025), read in full: an Australian National University art historian's essay on later uses of his 1857 painting 'The Arrest of Diponegoro'; says he is sometimes claimed as Indonesia's first modern painter though he died decades before the first nationalist movement, served as court painter to the Dutch governor-general and several European courts, long seen as a weak copy of Pieneman's picture and now argued to have reworked it, the painting now in the Istana Negara and returned by the Dutch government in 1978; records that 1976 and 1996 writers disagreed about his patriotism. Used for critical context and for the painting's facts; the political readings are not scored.

Peter Carey, 'Raden Saleh Syarif Bustaman (circa 1811-1880) and the Java War (1825-30): A Dissident Family History', Archipel 103 (2022), pp. 87-126, first 100,000 characters read: a historian's study of his childhood and family (guardianship in Semarang, apprenticeship to the Belgian painter Payen from about 1819-24), noting that his whereabouts in September 1825 are unclear and that most documented material concerns relatives; says that on return to a transformed Java the Dutch regarded him as belonging fully to neither Arab-Javanese nor Dutch society and that his later paintings may reflect his views of the colonial system. Scholarly and cautious; speculation about family trauma is not used.

adaptability.rationale: [src_saleh_rijks, src_saleh_qantara, src_saleh_jp_maestro, src_saleh_jp_kraus, src_saleh_carey | 1829-1852 | museum label + press + historian] The Rijksmuseum label says that after arriving in 1829 he soon specialised in oriental scenes and dressed as a Javanese prince, and that on Java he built a neo-Gothic palace and received the European elite, constantly shifting between Javanese and European identities; Qantara says he stayed in Dresden, learned several European languages (four or five) and worked independently on commissions; the Jakarta Post profile quotes him saying he came to Europe as a Javanese but returned to Java 'as a real German', and records discomfort in the Netherlands against acceptance in German homes; Carey says that on his return the Dutch regarded him as belonging fully to neither society. Movement between very different settings, with a cost on return, is documented, but the accounts are museum-label summary and curator-sourced press, hence moderate confidence.

cross_domain_range.rationale: [src_saleh_jp_exhibition, src_saleh_qantara, src_saleh_rijks, src_saleh_jp_kraus | 1829-1880 | press + museum label] The exhibition coverage says he was also an architect, landscape gardener and collector of ethnographic and archaeological documents; Qantara says he worked as a lay archaeologist and joined an expedition in Central Java after 1851; the Rijksmuseum label says he built a neo-Gothic palace on Java; Kraus (Jakarta Post 2013) says he founded his own school of landscape painting. The breadth is stated but described only in summary, painting remains the core, and the sources are promotional or popular, so the score is moderate and confidence modest.

mastery_orientation.rationale: [src_saleh_jp_kraus, src_saleh_jp_exhibition, src_saleh_qantara, src_saleh_sothebys | 1829-1852 | curator interview + press + auction note] Qantara says he trained for years in Europe on a government scholarship and then worked independently on commissions; the Sotheby's note says he was named 'King's Painter' in 1850 and studied the menagerie animals closely; Kraus says he was technically as good as or better than European contemporaries and that no other painter in the colony equalled him. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 68 / 0.50 because the judgements of quality come from the exhibition curator and an auction house with a stake in the work, and no independent critic's assessment of his training or craft was read.

deep_focus.rationale: [src_saleh_sothebys, src_saleh_qantara | c. 1830s-1850 | auction note quoting a contemporary letter + press] The Sotheby's note quotes a letter from his friend M. E. Verstege that Saleh lost his friendship for a time because he neglected his obligations, painting the animal trainer Henri Martin's portrait for free merely to be able to paint his lions; Qantara adds that he probably observed lions at a zoo or circus. Single-minded pursuit of a subject, at some cost to a friendship, is documented once through a quoted contemporary. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 66 / 0.50 because the behaviour rests on one letter relayed in a sales essay (with a misprinted date) and no other source describes the episode.

provenance.notes:
portrait_preflight: STRONG (lead-robust) (lead) / CONFIRMED WITH THE LEAD IMAGE: Rijksmuseum record SK-A-4703 opened live (linked-art JSON at https://id.rijksmuseum.nl/200107969, reached through the data.rijksmuseum.nl search by object number; the hdl.handle.net number guessed from the record was not used). The museum titles it 'Portrait of Raden Syarif Bustaman Saleh' (an earlier museum title, recorded in 2001, was 'Self-portrait'), states the painter as 'attributed to Friedrich Carl Albert Schreuel (1773-1853)', date c. 1840, oil on canvas 106.7 x 85.3 cm, acquired 1978 from a private seller, and gives the image the Public Domain Mark and the data CC0. Rights: whatever the exact hand, a c. 1840 painting by a painter who died in 1853 (or an unknown contemporary) is public domain by age, and the museum's own mark agrees; the record contains no restriction. Kind: historical_depiction, because the attribution is tentative, no documented sitting is recorded and the museum itself once catalogued it as a self-portrait; the sitter is positively named by the holder. The IIIF original (4884 x 6112 px) was downscaled to 959 x 1200 and never enlarged. The alternative photograph record NG-2011-31-30 (Woodbury & Page, 1863-66) is an album sheet of seven photographs whose small studio portraits are said to include two of Raden Saleh without indicating which, so it would have failed the positive-identification rule; it was only used to confirm the villa photograph exists.
PREFLIGHT: QID VERIFIED LIVE (2026-11-04): Wikidata wbgetentities Q1375979 returned en label 'Raden Saleh', description 'painter from Indonesia (1811-1880)', death 1880-04-23, birth recorded as 1811 (and 1814, 1807), Korean label '라덴 살레' (used as the display name; source: Wikidata Korean label). Birth year 1811 is used as the conventional date; sources disagree (1807-1814). SLUG/QID CHECK: not in prod64.txt and no existing candidate file. REGION south_asia: the repository has no Southeast Asian region and its Southeast Asian precedents (kartini ID, jose-rizal PH, ho-chi-minh VN, aung-san-suu-kyi MM) all use south_asia; nationality ID; era 19th_century. VOCABULARY: occupations painter and artist, field art, impact domains artistic and cultural, tags cross_disciplinary and craft_focused, archetype creative_creator, all with EN and KO labels. ZERO POLITICS: the contested political reading of the Arrest of Diponegoro (nationalist symbolism versus 'un-nationalistic') and his court-painter relations with the colonial government are context only and not scored; his family's Java War history (Carey) is likewise unscored.
ATTRIBUTION: confirmed (attributable): contemporary letters (Verstege), museum records and modern scholarship document his work and movements, although much of his own correspondence and a lost 300-page diary are not available.
CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Niken Prathivi, 'An encounter with Raden Saleh', The Jakarta Post, 13 January 2013 (interview with Werner Kraus) https://www.thejakartapost.com/news/2013/01/13/an-encounter-with-raden-saleh.html, with the Rijksmuseum label text for SK-A-4703 and the Qantara article.
SOURCES READ (8 substantive; Wikidata orientation only): Rijksmuseum label, Jakarta Post 2013 (Kraus interview), Jakarta Post 2012 exhibition article, Jakarta Post 2012 profile, Qantara, Sotheby's catalogue note, Elly Kent (National Gallery Singapore, critical), Peter Carey (Archipel 2022, scholarly). PERSPECTIVES: museum, curator-led press, popular feature, auction house, an independent art historian, a historian. COUNTER-VOICES/CAUTIONS: Kent (long seen as a weak copy; patriotism disputed in 1976 and 1996), Carey (Dutch regarded him as belonging to neither society; whereabouts in 1825 unclear), the Jakarta Post's note about allegations of widespread forgery of Indonesian masters. Weakness: the whole modern picture rests heavily on one curator (Kraus), his lost 300-page diary manuscript is unavailable, and nearly all behavioural material is secondhand; no score exceeds 72 and no confidence exceeds 0.58.
NOT OPENED: Kraus and Vogelsang's 2012 monograph (print), Kraus's 2005 Archipel article on the Arrest of Diponegoro, the Smarthistory and Britannica pages (HTTP 403, Cloudflare), IIAS Review (HTTP 403), Christie's lot essays (page returned only a sale calendar), the Passau page (404), the rest of Carey (last 37,000 characters unread), Wikipedia (orientation only). READ BUT NOT CITED: the Jakarta Post 19 June 2012 profile of Kraus (a passing curator remark that he was a big spender and jealous of rivals, not scored: secondhand character claims). EXCLUDED: freemasonry, marriages, spouses and death/illness details, the poisoning claim, the Dutch-return of the 1857 painting beyond one fact, the political interpretations, the claim that he added a noble 'von' to his name (single popular source), the Delacroix/Vernet influence (the Sotheby's note and Wikipedia state it but Kraus is quoted as saying Saleh never mentioned Delacroix), and any first/only claim beyond what is attributed in card text.
SELECTIVE SELF-CALIBRATION: reviewed mastery_orientation (lowered 68/0.50 to 62/0.44: judgements from the curator and an auction house), deep_focus (lowered 66/0.50 to 62/0.44: single letter in a sales essay), adaptability (kept: five sources across museum, press and a historian agree on the movement between settings and its cost), cross_domain_range (kept at moderate confidence already). Initial rows 4; lowered 2. Profile is deliberately sparse.

portrait.source: Oil painting 'Portrait of Raden Syarif Bustaman Saleh', attributed by the museum to Friedrich Carl Albert Schreuel (1773-1853), about 1840, 106.7 x 85.3 cm, Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam, object SK-A-4703 (acquired 1978); the museum released the image under its Public Domain Mark and the data record under CC0. The sitter is named by the museum. The museum scan was 4884 x 6112 pixels; this project reduced it to 959 x 1200 pixels, never enlarging it
